paragraphs: I had borne Fortunato’s thousand injuries as well as I could. But when he dared to insult me, I swore revenge. You, who know my soul so well, will not suppose that I spoke any threat aloud. In time, I would have my revenge. That was settled beyond doubt—but the very firmness of my decision ruled out the idea of risk. I must not only punish him, but escape punishment myself. A wrong remains unavenged when punishment overtakes the avenger. It is equally unavenged if he fails to make the wrongdoer understand that he is taking revenge.

You must understand that neither in word nor deed had I given Fortunato any reason to doubt my goodwill. I continued to smile in his face, as usual. He did not realise that I was now smiling at the thought of sacrificing him.

This Fortunato had a weak point, although in other respects he was a man to be respected and even feared. He prided himself on his expert knowledge of wine. Few Italians have a true love and understanding of the arts. For the most part, they put on enthusiasm to suit the moment and the opportunity, so they can deceive British and Austrian millionaires. In painting and precious stones, Fortunato was a fraud, like his countrymen. But where old wines were concerned, he was sincere. In this, I was not very different from him. I knew Italian vintages well myself and bought them in quantity whenever I could.

I met my friend at about dusk one evening, during the wildest madness of the carnival season. He greeted me with excessive warmth, for he had drunk a great deal. He wore a jester’s costume: a tight-fitting outfit with multicoloured stripes and a pointed cap with bells. I was so pleased to see him that I thought I would never finish wringing his hand.
I said to him, “My dear Fortunato, how lucky to meet you. You look remarkably well today! But I have received a large cask of what is supposed to be Amontillado, and I have my doubts.”
“What?” he said. “Amontillado? A cask? Impossible! And in the middle of the carnival!”
“I have my doubts,” I replied. “And I was foolish enough to pay the full price for Amontillado without consulting you. You were nowhere to be found, and I was afraid of losing a bargain.”
“Amontillado!”
“I have my doubts.”
“Amontillado!”
“And I must put them to rest.”
“Amontillado!”
“Since you are busy, I am on my way to Luchesi. If anyone has a discerning palate, he does. He will tell me—”
“Luchesi cannot tell Amontillado from sherry.”
“And yet some fools insist that his taste is as good as yours.”
“Come, let’s go.”
“Where?”
“To your vaults.”
“No, my friend. I will not take advantage of your kindness. I see that you have somewhere to be. Luchesi—”
“I have nowhere to be. Come.”
“No, my friend. It is not that, but the severe cold I can see you are suffering from. The vaults are unbearably damp. They are crusted with saltpetre deposits.”
“Let’s go all the same. The cold is nothing. Amontillado! You have been cheated. And as for Luchesi, he cannot tell sherry from Amontillado.”
As he spoke, Fortunato took my arm. I put on a black silk mask, drew my long cloak closely around me, and let him hurry me to my mansion.

No servants were at home. They had slipped away to enjoy the festivities. I had told them I would not return until morning and had explicitly ordered them not to leave the house. I knew very well that these orders would ensure that every one of them disappeared as soon as my back was turned.

I took two torches from their wall brackets and gave one to Fortunato. Bowing, I ushered him through several suites of rooms to the archway leading into the vaults. I went down a long, winding staircase and asked him to be careful as he followed. At last, we reached the bottom and stood together on the damp ground of the Montresors’ catacombs.
My friend walked unsteadily, and the bells on his cap jingled as he strode along.
“The cask,” he said.
“It is further on,” I said. “But notice the white web that gleams on these cavern walls.”
He turned towards me and met my gaze with clouded eyes watering with drunkenness.
“Saltpetre?” he asked at last.
“Saltpetre,” I replied. “How long have you had that cough?”
“Ugh! Ugh! Ugh!—ugh! Ugh! Ugh!—ugh! Ugh! Ugh!—ugh! Ugh! Ugh!—ugh! Ugh! Ugh!”
My poor friend could not answer for many minutes.
“It is nothing,” he said at last.

“Come,” I said firmly. “We will go back. Your health is precious. You are rich, respected, admired, loved. You are happy, as I once was. People would miss you. I do not matter. We will go back. You will become ill, and I cannot be responsible. Besides, there is Luchesi—”
“Enough,” he said. “The cough is nothing. It will not kill me. I shall not die of a cough.”
“True, true,” I replied. “Indeed, I had no intention of alarming you unnecessarily. But you should take every proper precaution. A drink of this Medoc will protect us from the damp.”
I took a bottle from a long row of others lying on the earth and knocked off its neck.
“Drink,” I said, offering him the wine.
He raised it to his lips with a leer. He paused and nodded to me familiarly, his bells jingling.
“I drink,” he said, “to the dead who rest around us.”
“And I to your long life.”
He took my arm again, and we went on.
“These vaults,” he said, “are very extensive.”
“The Montresors,” I replied, “were a great family, with many members.”
“I forget your coat of arms.”
“An enormous golden human foot against a blue background. The foot crushes a rearing serpent whose fangs are embedded in the heel.”
“And the motto?”
“No one attacks me and goes unpunished.”
“Good!” he said.

The wine made his eyes sparkle, and the bells jingled. The Medoc warmed my imagination too. We had passed between walls of piled bones, mixed with casks and large barrels, into the deepest parts of the catacombs. I stopped again, and this time took the liberty of seizing Fortunato’s arm above the elbow.

“The saltpetre!” I said. “Look, there is more of it. It hangs like moss from the vaults. We are below the riverbed. Drops of moisture trickle among the bones. Come, we will go back before it is too late. Your cough—”
“It is nothing,” he said. “Let’s go on. But first, another drink of the Medoc.”
I broke open a large bottle of De Grâve and handed it to him. He drained it in one breath. His eyes flashed fiercely. He laughed and threw the bottle upwards with a gesture I did not understand.
I looked at him in surprise. He repeated the movement, a grotesque one.
“You do not understand?” he said.
“I do not,” I replied.
“Then you are not one of the brotherhood.”
“What?”
“You are not one of the masons.”
“Yes, yes,” I said. “Yes, yes.”
“You? Impossible! A mason?”
“A mason,” I replied.
“Show me a sign,” he said.
“Here it is,” I answered, pulling a trowel from beneath the folds of my cloak.
“You are joking,” he exclaimed, recoiling several steps. “But let’s go on to the Amontillado.”

“Very well,” I said. I put the tool back under my cloak and offered him my arm again. He leaned heavily on it. We continued in search of the Amontillado. We passed through a series of low arches, went down, moved on, and went down again, until we reached a deep crypt. The air was so foul that our torches gave off more glow than flame.

At the farthest end of the crypt was another, smaller one. Its walls had been lined with human remains, piled up to the vaulted ceiling, like those in the great catacombs of Paris. Three sides of this inner crypt were still decorated that way. On the fourth, the bones had been thrown down and lay scattered on the earth, forming a sizeable mound in one place. In the wall exposed by removing the bones, we saw a recess still further inside. It was about four feet deep, three feet wide, and six or seven feet high. It seemed to have been built for no particular purpose of its own, merely forming the space between two of the enormous supports for the catacombs’ roof. At its back stood one of the catacombs’ enclosing walls of solid granite.
Fortunato raised his dim torch and tried in vain to peer into the recess. Its weak light did not let us see the back.
“Go on,” I said. “The Amontillado is in here. As for Luchesi—”

“He is an ignorant fool,” my friend interrupted, stepping unsteadily forward while I followed close on his heels. In an instant, he had reached the back of the recess. Finding his way blocked by rock, he stood in stupid bewilderment. A moment later, I had chained him to the granite. Two iron loops were fixed into its surface, side by side, about two feet apart. A short chain hung from one, and a padlock from the other. I passed the chain around his waist and secured it in a few seconds. He was too astonished to resist. Removing the key, I stepped back out of the recess.

“Run your hand over the wall,” I said. “You cannot help feeling the saltpetre. It is very damp indeed. Once more, let me beg you to return. No? Then I really must leave you. But first I must give you every little attention I can.”
“The Amontillado!” my friend burst out, still not recovered from his astonishment.
“True,” I replied. “The Amontillado.”

As I spoke, I set to work among the pile of bones I mentioned earlier. Throwing them aside, I soon uncovered a supply of building stone and mortar. With these materials and my trowel, I began vigorously to wall up the entrance to the recess.

I had barely laid the first row of stones when I realised that Fortunato had largely sobered up. The first sign was a low, moaning cry from deep inside the recess. It was not the cry of a drunken man. A long, stubborn silence followed. I laid the second row, then the third and fourth. Then I heard the chain shaking furiously. The noise lasted several minutes. To listen with greater satisfaction, I stopped work and sat down on the bones. When the clanking finally faded, I took up my trowel again and finished the fifth, sixth, and seventh rows without interruption. The wall was now nearly as high as my chest. I paused once more and held the torches over the masonry, casting a few weak rays onto the figure inside.

A series of loud, piercing screams suddenly burst from the chained figure’s throat and seemed to drive me violently backwards. For a brief moment, I hesitated. I trembled. Drawing my rapier, I began to feel about the recess with it, but a moment’s thought reassured me. I laid my hand on the solid structure of the catacombs and felt satisfied. I approached the wall again. I answered his yells. I echoed them, added to them, surpassed them in volume and force. As I did so, he grew silent.

It was midnight now, and my work was nearly finished. I had completed the eighth, ninth, and tenth rows. I had built part of the eleventh and last. Only one stone remained to be fitted and sealed in with mortar. Struggling with its weight, I worked it part of the way into position. But then a low laugh came from the recess, making the hair on my head stand up. A sad voice followed, which I could hardly recognise as that of the noble Fortunato. It said—
“Ha! Ha! Ha!—he! He!—a very good joke indeed, an excellent joke. We will have many a hearty laugh about it at the mansion—he! He! He!—over our wine—he! He! He!”
“The Amontillado!” I said.
“He! He! He!—he! He! He!—yes, the Amontillado. But isn’t it getting late? Won’t Lady Fortunato and the others be waiting for us at the mansion? Let’s go.”
“Yes,” I said. “Let’s go.”
“For the love of God, Montressor!”
“Yes,” I said. “For the love of God!”
But I listened in vain for an answer to those words. I grew impatient and called out—
“Fortunato!”
No answer. I called again—
“Fortunato!”

Still no answer. I pushed a torch through the remaining opening and let it fall inside. The only response was a jingling of bells. My heart felt sick—because of the dampness of the catacombs. I hurried to finish my work. I forced the last stone into place and sealed it with mortar. Against the new masonry, I rebuilt the old rampart of bones. For half a century, no mortal has disturbed them. May he rest in peace!
